questions.q: In his Sulba-Sutra, how does Baudhayana make a square with double the area of a given square?
questions.a: He draws a new square on the diagonal of the given square.
o: He draws a new square on the diagonal of the given square.
He doubles the length of each side of the given square.
He draws a new square on half of the diagonal of the given square.
He joins the midpoints of the sides of the given square.

questions.q: A square floor tile has an area of 18 sq cm. A new square is drawn on the diagonal of the tile. What is the area of the new square?
questions.a: 36 sq cm

questions.q: Rohit has a square sheet of paper of side 10 cm. He wants a square with exactly half the area of the sheet. Which method gives it?
questions.a: Fold all four corners to the centre, creasing through side midpoints.
o: Fold all four corners to the centre, creasing through side midpoints.
Cut out a square of side 5 cm from one corner of the whole sheet.
Cut the sheet along one diagonal and keep one of the two triangles.
Fold the sheet once along the line joining midpoints of opposite sides.

questions.q: (a) State Baudhayana's rule for making a square with double the area of a given square. (b) A square courtyard has an area of 45 sq m. What is the area of the square built on its diagonal?
questions.a: (a) The square built on the diagonal of a given square has double the area of the given square. (b) 2 x 45 = 90 sq m.
s: States that the square on the diagonal has double the area of the given square
Finds the area of the square on the diagonal as 90 sq m

questions.q: A square sheet of paper has a side of 12 cm. (a) Find the area of the sheet. (b) The corners are folded to the centre so that the creases pass through the midpoints of the sides. What is the area of the tilted square formed by the creases? (c) Find the area of a square of side 6 cm, and say how many such squares would fill the sheet.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 12 = 144 sq cm. (b) The crease square has half the area: 144 / 2 = 72 sq cm. (c) 6 x 6 = 36 sq cm, and 144 / 36 = 4 such squares fill the sheet, so halving the side gives a quarter of the area, not half.
s: Finds the area of the sheet as 144 sq cm
Finds the area of the crease square as 72 sq cm (half the sheet)
Finds 36 sq cm and says 4 such squares fill the sheet

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If each side of a square is doubled, the area of the square is doubled.
Reason (R): The area of a square is its side multiplied by itself.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: True or False: 'The tilted square made by joining the midpoints of the sides of a square of side 8 cm has a side of 4 cm.' Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The tilted square has half the area of the 8 cm square, that is 64 / 2 = 32 sq cm. A square of side 4 cm has an area of only 16 sq cm, a quarter of 64, so the side of the tilted square is not 4 cm (it is the number whose square is 32, between 5 and 6 cm).
s: States the verdict False
Shows the tilted square has area 32 sq cm while a 4 cm square has area 16 sq cm, so the side is not 4 cm

questions.q: In the doubling figure, a square is made of 2 small congruent triangles, and the square on its diagonal is made of 4 of the same triangles. Priya starts with a square of area 7 sq cm and draws a square on the diagonal three times in a row, each time on the newest square. She claims: 'My last square has an area of 56 sq cm and it is made of 32 of the small triangles of my first square.' Check both parts of her claim.
questions.a: Areas: 7, then 14, then 28, then 56 sq cm, so the area part is right. Triangles: 2, then 4, then 8, then 16, so the last square is made of 16 small triangles, not 32. Her claim is partly right: the area is correct but the count of triangles is wrong (each small triangle has area 3.5 sq cm, and 56 / 3.5 = 16).
s: Doubles the area three times to get 56 sq cm and agrees with the area part
Doubles the triangle count three times from 2 to get 16
Concludes the claim is partly right: area correct, 32 triangles wrong

questions.q:
A tile shop in Coimbatore sells a standard square tile of side 30 cm. A customer wants one large decorative tile with double the area of the standard tile for the centre of her hall, and some small tiles with half the area of the standard tile for the border. The shop worker makes the large tile as the square on the diagonal of a standard tile, and makes each small tile by joining the midpoints of the sides of a standard tile.
(a) Find the area of one standard tile.
(b) Find the area of the large tile.
(c) Find the area of one small tile.
(d) The customer says that one large tile and four small tiles together cover the same area as four standard tiles. Is she right? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) 30 x 30 = 900 sq cm. (b) Double the area: 2 x 900 = 1800 sq cm. (c) Half the area: 900 / 2 = 450 sq cm. (d) Yes: 1800 + 4 x 450 = 1800 + 1800 = 3600 sq cm, and 4 x 900 = 3600 sq cm, so the areas are equal.
s: (a) Finds the standard tile area as 900 sq cm
(b) Finds the large tile area as 1800 sq cm
(c) Finds the small tile area as 450 sq cm
(d) Finds 3600 sq cm for both and says she is right

questions.q: Start with a square of side 3 cm. Draw a square on its diagonal, then a square on the diagonal of that new square, and so on, each time using the newest square. (a) Find the area of the first square. (b) Find the areas of the second and third squares. (c) Find the side of the third square and compare it with the side of the first square. (d) Explain why drawing the square on the diagonal twice in a row always doubles the side. (e) Without listing every area, find the side of the square you get after 6 such steps from the first square, and check your answer using its area.
questions.a: (a) 3 x 3 = 9 sq cm. (b) 18 sq cm and 36 sq cm. (c) 6 x 6 = 36, so the third square has side 6 cm, twice the first side of 3 cm. (d) Two steps multiply the area by 2 x 2 = 4, and a square with 4 times the area has twice the side, because (2s) x (2s) = 4 x s x s. (e) 6 steps are three pairs of steps, so the side doubles three times: 3, 6, 12, 24 cm. Check: the area is 9 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 576 sq cm, and 24 x 24 = 576.
s: (a) Finds the first area as 9 sq cm
(b) Finds the second and third areas as 18 and 36 sq cm
(c) Finds the third side 6 cm, twice the first side
(d) Explains that two steps make the area 4 times, so the side doubles
(e) Finds the side 24 cm after 6 steps and checks 24 x 24 = 576 = 9 x 64

questions.q: In a right triangle, what is the side opposite the right angle called?
questions.a: The hypotenuse

questions.q: An isosceles right triangle has equal sides of 5 cm. What is the area of the square drawn on its hypotenuse?
questions.a: 50 sq cm

questions.q:
Each row of Column A gives the equal sides a of an isosceles right triangle. Match it with c x c in Column B, where c is the hypotenuse.
Column A: 1. a = 13 2. a = 15 3. a = 17 4. a = 19
Column B: A. 578 B. 722 C. 338 D. 450
(a) What is an isosceles right triangle? Write the relation between its equal sides a and its hypotenuse c. (b) Use the relation to find c x c when a = 1, and say what c is.
questions.a: (a) It is a right triangle whose two sides that form the right angle are equal. The relation is c x c = 2 x a x a. (b) c x c = 2 x 1 x 1 = 2, so c = √2.
s: Describes the triangle (right angle, two equal sides) and writes c x c = 2 x a x a
Finds c x c = 2 and c = √2 for a = 1

questions.q: A square scarf is folded along one diagonal to make an isosceles right triangle. The longest side of this triangle measures 14 cm. (a) Using c x c = 2 x a x a, find a x a, where a is the side of the scarf. (b) Between which two whole numbers of centimetres does the side of the scarf lie?
questions.a: (a) 14 x 14 = 196 = 2 x a x a, so a x a = 98 (this is also the area of the scarf in sq cm). (b) 9 x 9 = 81 and 10 x 10 = 100, and 81 < 98 < 100, so the side lies between 9 cm and 10 cm.
s: Uses c = 14 to get 2 x a x a = 196 and a x a = 98
Compares 98 with 81 and 100 to place a between 9 and 10 cm

questions.q: An isosceles right triangle has equal sides of 16 cm. (a) Find c x c, where c is its hypotenuse. (b) Find the two consecutive whole numbers between which c lies. (c) Find the area of the triangle.
questions.a: (a) c x c = 2 x 16 x 16 = 512. (b) 22 x 22 = 484 and 23 x 23 = 529, so c lies between 22 cm and 23 cm. (c) Area = half of 16 x 16 = 256 / 2 = 128 sq cm.
s: Finds c x c = 512
Uses 484 and 529 to place c between 22 and 23 cm
Finds the area as 128 sq cm

questions.q: Sohan says: 'The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is twice as long as each equal side, so if the hypotenuse is 20 cm, each equal side is 10 cm.' Check his claim using c x c = 2 x a x a, and find the equal side correct to one decimal place, as a pair of bounds.
questions.a: No. If a = 10, then c x c = 2 x 100 = 200, but 20 x 20 = 400, so the hypotenuse is not twice the side. With c = 20: 2 x a x a = 400, so a x a = 200. 14 x 14 = 196 and 15 x 15 = 225, so a is between 14 and 15; 14.1 x 14.1 = 198.81 and 14.2 x 14.2 = 201.64, so 14.1 cm < a < 14.2 cm.
s: Shows that a = 10 gives c x c = 200, not 400, so the claim is wrong
Finds a x a = 200 and places a between 14 and 15
Squares 14.1 and 14.2 to give 14.1 < a < 14.2

questions.q:
An isosceles right triangle has equal sides of 6 units. Consider these statements.
Statement I: The square on its hypotenuse has an area of 72 sq units.
Statement II: Its hypotenuse lies between 8 and 9 units.
Statement III: The area of the triangle is 36 sq units.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: A carpenter cuts square wooden boards along one diagonal to make isosceles right-triangle shelf brackets. One board has a side of 20 cm. (a) Find the area of the square on the hypotenuse of a bracket from this board. (b) Between which two whole numbers of centimetres is the hypotenuse? (c) Find the area of one bracket. (d) For another bracket, the square on the hypotenuse has an area of 392 sq cm. Find the equal sides of that bracket.
questions.a: (a) c x c = 2 x 20 x 20 = 800 sq cm. (b) 28 x 28 = 784 and 29 x 29 = 841, so the hypotenuse is between 28 cm and 29 cm. (c) Half the board: 400 / 2 = 200 sq cm. (d) 2 x a x a = 392, so a x a = 196 and a = 14 cm.
s: (a) Finds the area of the square on the hypotenuse as 800 sq cm
(b) Uses 784 and 841 to place the hypotenuse between 28 and 29 cm
(c) Finds the bracket area as 200 sq cm
(d) Solves 2 x a x a = 392 to get a = 14 cm

questions.q: A school is making a garden in a corner where two walls meet at a right angle. The garden will be an isosceles right triangle, and only its longest side (along the path) needs fencing. Fencing costs Rs 450 per metre and is sold only in whole metres. Plan A: the equal sides along the walls are 10 m each. Plan B: the fenced side is exactly 12 m. (a) For Plan A, find c x c for the fenced side. (b) How many whole metres of fencing must be bought for Plan A? (c) For Plan B, find the square of each equal side and the two whole numbers between which the equal side lies. (d) Find the garden area for each option. (e) The school wants the most garden area for each rupee spent on fencing. Which option should it choose? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) c x c = 2 x 10 x 10 = 200. (b) 14 x 14 = 196 < 200 < 225 = 15 x 15, so the side is between 14 and 15 m and 15 m must be bought. (c) 2 x a x a = 144, so a x a = 72; 64 < 72 < 81, so a is between 8 and 9 m. (d) A: 10 x 10 / 2 = 50 sq m; B: a x a / 2 = 72 / 2 = 36 sq m. (e) A costs 15 x 450 = Rs 6,750 for 50 sq m, Rs 135 per sq m; B costs 12 x 450 = Rs 5,400 for 36 sq m, Rs 150 per sq m. Plan A gives more area per rupee, so the school should choose A (although B is cheaper in total).
s: (a) Finds c x c = 200 for Plan A
(b) Places the side between 14 and 15 m and says 15 m must be bought
(c) Finds a x a = 72 and a between 8 and 9 m for Plan B
(d) Finds the areas 50 sq m and 36 sq m
(e) Compares Rs 135 and Rs 150 per sq m and chooses Plan A

questions.q: Between which two whole numbers does √2 lie?
questions.a: 1 and 2

questions.q: 1.41 x 1.41 = 1.9881 and 1.42 x 1.42 = 2.0164. What do these two results show about √2?
Anu tests the fraction 7/5 as a value for √2. She finds (7/5) x (7/5) = 49/25 = 1.96. What can she correctly conclude?
questions.a: 7/5 is less than √2.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle whose equal sides are 1 m long is longer than 1.4 m.
Reason (R): 1.4 x 1.4 = 1.96, which is less than 2.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Find 1.3 x 1.3 and 1.5 x 1.5. (b) Use your answers to say whether √2 lies between 1.3 and 1.5.
questions.a: (a) 1.3 x 1.3 = 1.69 and 1.5 x 1.5 = 2.25. (b) Yes. Since 1.69 < 2 < 2.25, the number whose square is 2 lies between 1.3 and 1.5.
s: Finds 1.69 and 2.25
Uses 1.69 < 2 < 2.25 to say √2 lies between 1.3 and 1.5

questions.q: True or False: 'A square whose side is √2 units long has an area of exactly 2 square units.' Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The area of a square is side x side, and √2 is the number whose square is 2, so √2 x √2 = 2 square units exactly. (It is the square drawn on the diagonal of a unit square.)
s: States the verdict True
Explains that side x side = √2 x √2 = 2, since √2 is the number whose square is 2

questions.q: Pooja knows that 1.414 < √2 < 1.415. She says: 'So the diagonal of a square of side 3 m lies between 4.242 m and 4.245 m.' Check her claim (a) by finding c x c for the diagonal, and (b) by squaring 4.242 and 4.245. (c) Say whether she is right.
questions.a: (a) The diagonal c satisfies c x c = 2 x 3 x 3 = 18 (so c = 3 x √2). (b) 4.242 x 4.242 = 17.994564 and 4.245 x 4.245 = 18.020025. (c) She is right: 17.994564 < 18 < 18.020025, so 4.242 m < c < 4.245 m. Multiplying 1.414 < √2 < 1.415 by 3 gives the same bounds.
s: (a) Finds c x c = 18 for the diagonal
(c) Compares with 18 and agrees that the claim is right

questions.q: Show that √2 cannot be equal to the fraction 99/70. Do it in two ways: (a) by comparing 2 x 70 x 70 with 99 x 99, and (b) by counting how many times the prime 2 occurs in the prime factorisation of each of these two numbers.
questions.a: If √2 = 99/70, then 2 = (99 x 99)/(70 x 70), so 2 x 70 x 70 = 99 x 99. (a) But 2 x 70 x 70 = 9800 and 99 x 99 = 9801, which are not equal. (b) 70 = 2 x 5 x 7, so 70 x 70 has the prime 2 twice and 2 x 70 x 70 has it three times (an odd number); 99 = 3 x 3 x 11 has no 2, so 99 x 99 has 2 zero times (an even number). The two sides can never be equal, so √2 is not 99/70.
s: Writes the condition 2 x 70 x 70 = 99 x 99 that √2 = 99/70 would need
(a) Finds 9800 and 9801 and notes they differ
(b) Counts the prime 2 three times (odd) on one side and zero times (even) on the other

questions.q:
The maths club of a school in Pune is making a poster called 'Hunting for √2'. √2 is the side of a square of area 2 sq units, so the club squares decimals to trap it. Their notebook already shows 1.3 x 1.3 = 1.69 and 1.5 x 1.5 = 2.25. A teacher also gives them 1.414 x 1.414 = 1.999396 and 1.415 x 1.415 = 2.002225.
(a) Find 1.4 x 1.4 and write bounds for √2 with one decimal place.
(b) Find 1.41 x 1.41 and 1.42 x 1.42, and write bounds for √2 with two decimal places.
(c) Use the teacher's values to write bounds for √2 with three decimal places.
(d) One member wants to keep squaring longer and longer decimals until a square comes out exactly 2. Will the club ever finish? Justify your answer.
questions.a: (a) 1.4 x 1.4 = 1.96 < 2 < 2.25 = 1.5 x 1.5, so 1.4 < √2 < 1.5. (b) 1.41 x 1.41 = 1.9881 and 1.42 x 1.42 = 2.0164, so 1.41 < √2 < 1.42. (c) 1.999396 < 2 < 2.002225, so 1.414 < √2 < 1.415. (d) No. A terminating decimal ends in a non-zero last digit, and its square then also ends in a non-zero digit after the decimal point, so it can never be 2.000... exactly. The decimal for √2 goes on forever, so the club can only keep narrowing the bounds.
s: (a) Finds 1.96 and gives 1.4 < √2 < 1.5
(c) Gives 1.414 < √2 < 1.415 from the teacher's values
(d) Says no, using the non-zero last digit argument that √2 is non-terminating

questions.q: This question checks why √2 cannot be a terminating decimal. (a) Find 1.4144 x 1.4144 and write its last digit after the decimal point. (b) For each last digit 1, 2, 3, ..., 9 of a number, write the last digit of its square. (c) Use (b) to explain why the square of a decimal whose last digit is non-zero always has a non-zero last digit after the decimal point. (d) Explain why this means no terminating decimal can have a square exactly equal to 2. (e) A calculator shows √2 as 1.41421356. Is this the exact value of √2? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 1.4144 x 1.4144 = 2.00052736; its last digit is 6. (b) 1 gives 1, 2 gives 4, 3 gives 9, 4 gives 6, 5 gives 5, 6 gives 6, 7 gives 9, 8 gives 4, 9 gives 1. (c) The last digit of the square comes only from last digit x last digit, and none of the results in (b) ends in 0, so the square has a non-zero last digit after the decimal point. (d) 2 written as a decimal is 2.000..., with no non-zero digit after the point, so a terminating decimal (non-zero last digit) can never square to exactly 2. (e) No. 1.41421356 is a terminating decimal, so by (d) its square is not exactly 2; the calculator shows only the first few digits of a decimal that goes on forever.
s: (a) Finds 2.00052736 with last digit 6
(b) Lists the last digits 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1
(c) Explains that no last digit squares to a number ending in 0
(d) Concludes no terminating decimal squares to exactly 2.000...
(e) Says the calculator value is not exact, because it is a terminating decimal

questions.q: According to the chapter, who was the first person in history to state the theorem on right-angled triangles (a x a + b x b = c x c) in this general form?
questions.a: Baudhayana

questions.q: A cyclist rides 24 km due north and then 10 km due east. How far is she from her starting point in a straight line?
questions.a: 26 km

questions.q: A 2.5 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is on level ground, 0.7 m from the wall. How high up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?

Consider these statements about Baudhayana's method of combining two squares into one.
Statement I: The area of the combined square is the sum of the areas of the two given squares.
Statement II: The side of the combined square is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose perpendicular sides are the sides of the two given squares.
Statement III: When the two given squares are the same size, the combined square is the square on the diagonal of either of them.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III

questions.q: A right triangle has shorter sides of 9 cm and 12 cm. (a) Find c x c, where c is the hypotenuse. (b) Find c.
s: Finds c x c = 81 + 144 = 225
Finds c = 15 cm

questions.q: (a) State Baudhayana's theorem on right-angled triangles. (b) Give one example of three whole-number side lengths of a right triangle mentioned in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) If a right-angled triangle has side lengths a, b and c, where c is the length of the hypotenuse, then a x a + b x b = c x c. (b) For example 3, 4 and 5 (or 5, 12 and 13), since 9 + 16 = 25.
s: States a x a + b x b = c x c with c the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle
Gives a correct whole-number example such as 3, 4, 5

questions.q: The sloping plank of a loading ramp is 3.7 m long and its top end is 1.2 m above the ground. The vertical height and the ground are at right angles. (a) Find the square of the horizontal distance covered by the ramp. (b) Find that horizontal distance.
questions.a: (a) The plank is the hypotenuse, so b x b = 3.7 x 3.7 - 1.2 x 1.2 = 13.69 - 1.44 = 12.25. (b) 3.5 x 3.5 = 12.25, so the horizontal distance is 3.5 m.
s: Treats the plank as the hypotenuse and finds b x b = 13.69 - 1.44 = 12.25
Finds the horizontal distance as 3.5 m

questions.q: A farmer has two square plots of sides 5 m and 12 m. He wants to exchange them for one square plot with the same total area, using Baudhayana's method. (a) Find the total area of the two plots. (b) Find the side of the new square plot. (c) Is the side of the new plot equal to 5 m + 12 m? Show the difference.
questions.a: (a) 5 x 5 + 12 x 12 = 25 + 144 = 169 sq m. (b) 13 x 13 = 169, so the side is 13 m (the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides 5 m and 12 m). (c) No. 5 + 12 = 17 m, which is 4 m more than 13 m; a square of side 17 m would have area 289 sq m.
s: Finds the total area 169 sq m
Finds the side of the new plot as 13 m
Says no, comparing 13 m with 17 m

questions.q: Neel says: 'If both shorter sides of a right triangle are made 1 cm longer, the hypotenuse also becomes exactly 1 cm longer.' Test his claim with the right triangle of sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm.
questions.a: No. New shorter sides are 4 cm and 5 cm, so c x c = 16 + 25 = 41. If the hypotenuse were 1 cm longer it would be 6 cm, but 6 x 6 = 36, not 41. Since 36 < 41 < 49, the new hypotenuse lies between 6 cm and 7 cm, so it grows by more than 1 cm. The claim is false.
s: Finds the new c x c = 16 + 25 = 41
Compares with 6 x 6 = 36 and shows the hypotenuse is not 6 cm
Concludes the claim is false (the new hypotenuse is between 6 and 7 cm)

questions.q: Let a, b and c be the sides of a right triangle, with c the hypotenuse. Find the missing side in each case. (a) a = 16, b = 30 (b) a = 7, c = 25 (c) a = 12, b = 35 (d) b = 60, c = 61 (e) a = 0.6, b = 0.8
s: (a) Finds c = 34
(b) Finds b = 24
(c) Finds c = 37
(d) Finds a = 11
(e) Finds c = 1

questions.q: Fermat's Last Theorem says that x to the power n + y to the power n = z to the power n has no solution in natural numbers when n is greater than 2. Who proved it, and in which year?
questions.a: Andrew Wiles, in 1994

questions.q:
Assertion (A): (8, 15, 17) is a primitive Baudhayana triple.
Reason (R): Every number in a primitive Baudhayana triple is odd.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A Baudhayana triple (a, b, c) is three positive integers with a x a + b x b = c x c. Which of these is a Baudhayana triple?

In the odd-square method, an odd square k x k is the n-th odd number (k x k = 2n - 1), and (n - 1) x (n - 1) + k x k = n x n gives the triple (k, n - 1, n). Match each odd square in Column A with the triple it gives in Column B.
Column A: 1. 225 2. 361 3. 529 4. 625
Column B: A. (23, 264, 265) B. (25, 312, 313) C. (15, 112, 113) D. (19, 180, 181)

Consider these statements about Baudhayana triples.
Statement I: Every scaled version (ka, kb, kc) of a triple, with k greater than 1, is not primitive.
Statement II: (20, 21, 29) is a scaled version of a smaller Baudhayana triple.
Statement III: There are infinitely many Baudhayana triples.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: (a) Write the scaled version of the Baudhayana triple (5, 12, 13) with k = 4. (b) Check that your answer is a Baudhayana triple.
s: Writes the scaled triple (20, 48, 52)

questions.q: True or False: 'If a Baudhayana triple has a common factor f greater than 1, dividing all three numbers by f gives another Baudhayana triple.' Check it for (24, 70, 74).
questions.a: True. 24 x 24 + 70 x 70 = 576 + 4900 = 5476 = 74 x 74, and the common factor is 2. Dividing by 2 gives (12, 35, 37), and 144 + 1225 = 1369 = 37 x 37, so it is again a triple. In general, if (a, b, c) = (fx, fy, fz) then f x f x (x x x + y x y) = f x f x z x z, so x x x + y x y = z x z.
s: States the verdict True
Divides (24, 70, 74) by 2 to get (12, 35, 37) and checks 144 + 1225 = 1369

questions.q: Use the odd-square method with the odd square 49. (a) 49 is the n-th odd number, so 49 = 2n - 1. Find n. (b) Write the equation (n - 1) x (n - 1) + 49 = n x n for this n. (c) Write the Baudhayana triple you get.
s: Finds n = 25
Writes the triple (7, 24, 25)

questions.q:
A Class 8 team in Lucknow was asked to list every Baudhayana triple (a, b, c) with a < b < c and all numbers at most 30. Their list is: (3, 4, 5), (6, 8, 10), (5, 12, 13), (9, 12, 15), (8, 15, 17), (12, 16, 20), (15, 20, 25), (7, 24, 25), (10, 24, 26), (18, 24, 30). A primitive triple has no common factor greater than 1.
(a) Which triples in their list are primitive?
(b) Show that (18, 24, 30) is a scaled version of a primitive triple, and name it.
(c) Which primitive triples in their list could come from the odd-square method, where the largest number is 1 more than the middle one?
(d) The team says their list is complete. Check (20, 21, 29) and decide whether they are right.
questions.a: (a) (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17) and (7, 24, 25); every other triple in the list has a common factor greater than 1, for example 2 in (6, 8, 10) and 4 in (12, 16, 20). (b) 18, 24 and 30 have the common factor 6, and (18, 24, 30) = 6 x (3, 4, 5); 324 + 576 = 900 = 30 x 30. (c) (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13) and (7, 24, 25); (8, 15, 17) cannot, because 17 is 2 more than 15. (d) 20 x 20 + 21 x 21 = 400 + 441 = 841 = 29 x 29, and all three numbers are at most 30, so (20, 21, 29) is a missing triple (a primitive one). The team is wrong: the list is not complete.
s: (a) Names the four primitive triples (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25)
(c) Names (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (7, 24, 25) and explains why (8, 15, 17) cannot come from the method
(d) Checks 400 + 441 = 841 and decides the list is not complete

questions.q: In his Sulba-Sutra, Baudhayana lists these triples: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), (12, 35, 37) and (15, 36, 39). (a) Check that (12, 35, 37) is a Baudhayana triple. (b) Show that (15, 36, 39) is not primitive and find the primitive triple it is a scaled version of. (c) Which of the six triples are primitive? (d) In the odd-square method the triple is (k, n - 1, n), so the largest number is always 1 more than the middle one. Which of the primitive triples in the list can the method produce? (e) Explain why the method can never produce (12, 35, 37), and say what this tells you about whether the method finds every primitive triple.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 12 + 35 x 35 = 144 + 1225 = 1369 = 37 x 37. (b) 15, 36 and 39 share the factor 3, and (15, 36, 39) = 3 x (5, 12, 13). (c) (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25) and (12, 35, 37); each has no common factor greater than 1. (d) (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13) and (7, 24, 25). (e) In (12, 35, 37) the largest number is 2 more than the middle one, while the method always gives a difference of 1, so it can never produce it (the same holds for (8, 15, 17)). So there are primitive triples that the odd-square method does not find.
s: (b) Shows the common factor 3 and (15, 36, 39) = 3 x (5, 12, 13)
(c) Names the five primitive triples
(e) Uses the difference of 2 to explain why (12, 35, 37) is missed and concludes the method does not find every primitive triple

questions.q: A rectangular door frame is 15 dm wide and 8 dm high, with right-angled corners. (a) Find the length of its diagonal. (b) Is the diagonal longer than both sides of the frame?
questions.a: (a) d x d = 15 x 15 + 8 x 8 = 225 + 64 = 289, and 17 x 17 = 289, so the diagonal is 17 dm. (b) Yes, 17 dm is longer than both 15 dm and 8 dm, because the diagonal is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by two sides.
s: Finds d x d = 289 and the diagonal 17 dm
Says yes, the diagonal (the hypotenuse) is longer than 15 dm and 8 dm

questions.q: True or False: 'A rhombus whose diagonals are 6 cm and 8 cm has sides of 10 cm.' The diagonals of a rhombus cut each other in half at right angles. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Each side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose shorter sides are HALF the diagonals, 3 cm and 4 cm. So side x side = 9 + 16 = 25 and the side is 5 cm. The value 10 cm comes from wrongly using the whole diagonals.
s: States the verdict False
Uses the half-diagonals 3 cm and 4 cm to find the side 5 cm

questions.q: An equilateral triangle has sides of 10 cm. Its altitude bisects the opposite side. (a) Find the lengths of the sides of the right triangle formed by the altitude, half the base and one side (leave the altitude as h). (b) Find h x h, and show by squaring 8.6 and 8.7 that 8.6 cm < h < 8.7 cm. (c) Use (b) to give bounds for the area of the triangle.
questions.a: (a) The right triangle has hypotenuse 10 cm (a side), one shorter side 5 cm (half the base) and the other shorter side h. (b) h x h = 100 - 25 = 75; 8.6 x 8.6 = 73.96 < 75 < 75.69 = 8.7 x 8.7, so 8.6 < h < 8.7. (c) Area = half x 10 x h = 5 x h, so the area lies between 5 x 8.6 = 43 sq cm and 5 x 8.7 = 43.5 sq cm.
s: (a) Identifies the right triangle: hypotenuse 10 cm, shorter sides 5 cm and h
(b) Finds h x h = 75 and checks 73.96 < 75 < 75.69
(c) Gives the area between 43 and 43.5 sq cm

questions.q: The diagonals of a rhombus cut each other in half at right angles. Show that a rhombus with sides of 5 cm can never have a diagonal of 10 cm or more.
questions.a: Half of each diagonal and a side form a right triangle with the side (5 cm) as the hypotenuse. Let the half-diagonals be p and q, so p x p + q x q = 25. Since q is more than 0, p x p is less than 25, so p is less than 5 cm: the hypotenuse is the longest side. So each diagonal, 2p, is less than 10 cm. A diagonal of 10 cm or more would make a half-diagonal at least 5 cm, as long as the hypotenuse, which is impossible.
s: Sets up the right triangle with half-diagonals p, q and hypotenuse 5 cm (p x p + q x q = 25)
Argues p x p < 25 so each half-diagonal is less than 5 cm (the hypotenuse is the longest side)
Concludes each diagonal is less than 10 cm

questions.q: A glass shop in Firozabad cuts rectangular panes and fixes a straight metal strip along one diagonal of each. The owner wants the two sides and the diagonal of every pane to be whole numbers of centimetres. (a) Show that a pane 24 cm by 32 cm has a whole-number diagonal. (b) Scale the triple (5, 12, 13) to give a pane with a diagonal of 39 cm. (c) Scale the triple (8, 15, 17) to give a pane with a diagonal of 51 cm. (d) Find two different panes, each with a diagonal of exactly 50 cm, by scaling two different primitive triples.
s: (a) Finds 576 + 1024 = 1600 and the diagonal 40 cm
(b) Scales (5, 12, 13) by 3 to get 15 cm by 36 cm
(c) Scales (8, 15, 17) by 3 to get 24 cm by 45 cm
(d) Gives 30 cm by 40 cm and 14 cm by 48 cm with a check

questions.q:
A school in Shimla wants to run a cable from the top of its 15 m tall building to the top of a 6 m tall pole. The pole stands upright on level ground, 12 m from the building. Route P is a straight cable from the top of the building to the top of the pole; it needs a support clamp costing Rs 400. Route Q runs the cable straight down the building wall to the height of the pole top and then horizontally to the pole. Cable costs Rs 85 per metre.
(a) How much higher is the top of the building than the top of the pole?
(b) Find the length of the cable for Route P.
(c) Find the length of the cable for Route Q.
(d) Which route is cheaper, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) 15 - 6 = 9 m. (b) Route P is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides 9 m and 12 m: 81 + 144 = 225 = 15 x 15, so 15 m. (c) Route Q is 9 m down plus 12 m across = 21 m. (d) P costs 15 x 85 + 400 = 1275 + 400 = Rs 1,675; Q costs 21 x 85 = Rs 1,785. Route P is cheaper by Rs 110, even with the clamp.
s: (a) Finds the height difference 9 m
(b) Uses 81 + 144 = 225 to get 15 m for Route P
(c) Finds 21 m for Route Q
(d) Finds Rs 1,675 and Rs 1,785 and chooses Route P, cheaper by Rs 110
